title: Bibi Amro
hookLine: Guru Angad's daughter whose dawn singing brought Amar Das to the Guru

lines: STILL DARK, A CHURN, A SONG.
cards: It's still dark. In a village house, a young woman sits at the churn, pulling the cord back and forth, turning milk into butter the way it was done every morning.
While her hands work, she sings, just enough to keep time with the churn. On the other side of the wall, an older man in the same family is awake too.
He's devout, and tradition says he has walked to the holy river many times in his life, still looking for something. He hears the words. He stops.
And he asks a question that will change the rest of his life: whose words are these?

teach.b: Bibi Amro was the daughter of Guru Angad, the second Guru, who sat in Guru Nanak's seat at Khadur. Tradition says she married into the family of a man named Amar Das and went to live in his village.
Amar Das was religious in the way of his time: he kept fasts, went on pilgrimage, was good and careful. But the story says he had never had a teacher.
Then one morning he heard his young relative singing at her work, a hymn of Guru Nanak. Tradition says the words went straight into him. He asked whose they were.

She told him plainly: these are Guru Nanak's words, and my father now sits in his place. Amar Das asked her to take him there, and she did. She brought him to Khadur, to her father, and he never really left.
The story says he stayed to serve Guru Angad for years, carrying water, doing the plain work of the house. And in time, Guru Angad chose him to be the next Guru: Guru Amar Das, the third.
Notice what Bibi Amro did, and what she didn't. She didn't argue with him. She didn't set out to convince anybody.
She was churning butter, and the song was part of her morning, as ordinary as the milk.

teach.h: FAITH THAT CARRIES THROUGH A WALL.
teach.b: Because it was real to her, it carried through a wall.
Sikhs remember her for faith that simply sounded while she worked. One woman singing at dawn, and the Guruship found its next keeper.

how: Sikhs remember Bibi Amro in the story of how Guru Amar Das came to Guru Angad, and some Sikh households still sing gurbani during ordinary work, at home and at dawn.

games.q: you're Amar Das. before dawn you hear a young relative singing words that go straight into you. what do you do?
o: keep quiet and go on with your own pilgrimages.
ask her whose words these are.
correct her for singing so early.
games.why: he asked, and she told him plainly: Guru Nanak's words. then he asked her to take him to her father, and his life turned.

practice: Bring to mind one song or line you love, sacred or not; if you know a shabad, you can use that. Let it run quietly in your head, in time with the breath, the way Bibi Amro kept time with the churn.

wordCard.voice: Bibi Amro. Guru Angad's daughter, whose song at dawn, tradition says, brought Amar Das to the Guru.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: Bibi Amro; Bibi is a respectful title for a woman.

carryVoice: Your line: her song changed a life. Not a sermon, just a morning. See you tomorrow.
